derivations.claim: For $n=0$ and $n=1$, the only allowed arc count is $p=0$; the all-defect link state has Gram matrix $(1)$, agreeing with the empty product.

For any $n$, the $p=0$ module is spanned by the all-defect state and its form value is $1$. Now fix $n\ge2$ and assume inductively that the determinant formula holds at all smaller ranks; because no positive quantum integer vanishes when $q^2$ is not a root of unity, those smaller Gram forms are nondegenerate.

Suppose $n>2p>0$. By [F2], restriction has the nondegenerate rightmost-defect submodule $W_{n-1,n-1-2p}$ and quotient $W_{n-1,n-1-2(p-1)}$. Invariance [F1] makes the orthogonal complement of the submodule invariant, and nondegeneracy gives a direct sum; projection identifies that complement with the quotient. The quotient is simple by [F3] and induction; its standard form is nondegenerate and invariant, hence makes it self-dual, so Schur's lemma [F4] makes the induced invariant form a scalar $\alpha_{n,p}$ times that standard form. Subtracting the submodule projection from each quotient lift is a block-triangular basis change with identity diagonal, so the Gram matrix in this basis is $G_{n-1,p}\oplus\alpha_{n,p}G_{n-1,p-1}$ and the change-of-basis determinant is $1$.

If $n=2p$ with $p>0$, deleting the rightmost endpoint and turning its partner into a defect bijects the link-state basis with that of $W_{2p-1,p-1}$. In the glued matching graph, the reduced pairing has one open path between the new defect ends; restoring the two terminal arcs closes exactly that path into one additional component and leaves every other component unchanged. Hence $G_{2p,p}=\delta G_{2p-1,p-1}$, which is the boundary scalar $\alpha_{2p,p}=\delta$.

For $n>2p$, refine the ordered link states into four types: type 1 has $n$ and $n-1$ both defects; type 2 has $n$ a defect and $n-1$ on an earlier arc; type 3 joins $n-1$ to $n$; and type 4 has $n$ on an arc whose partner is earlier than $n-1$. The gluing rule gives $G^{12}_{n,p}=\begin{pmatrix}0&*\\G_{n-2,p-1}&*\end{pmatrix}$ and $G^{22}_{n,p}=\begin{pmatrix}\delta G_{n-2,p-1}&*\\ *&*\end{pmatrix}$: the type-1/type-3 pairing has unmatched defects and is zero, cutting a type-2/type-3 terminal arc leaves the same exterior matching, and a type-3/type-3 pairing creates one loop. Let $A=G_{n-2,p}$, $B=G_{n-2,p-1}$, and write the rank-$(n-1)$ form as $G_{n-1,p}=\begin{pmatrix}A&AV_0\\V_0^{\mathsf T}A&V_0^{\mathsf T}AV_0+\alpha_{n-1,p}B\end{pmatrix}$; at $n=2p+1$ the $A,V_0$ blocks are empty and their products are omitted. If $V=\begin{pmatrix}V^{11}&*\\V^{21}&*\end{pmatrix}$ is the off-diagonal block in the orthogonalizing basis change of step 3.1, then $G^{12}_{n,p}=G_{n-1,p}V$ gives $0=AV^{11}+AV_0V^{21}$ and $B=V_0^{\mathsf T}AV^{11}+(V_0^{\mathsf T}AV_0+\alpha_{n-1,p}B)V^{21}$. The first equation gives $V^{11}=-V_0V^{21}$; substitution in the second cancels the $A$-terms and yields $B=\alpha_{n-1,p}BV^{21}$, so $V^{21}=\alpha_{n-1,p}^{-1}I$ since $B$ and $\alpha_{n-1,p}$ are nonzero for generic $q$.

The top-left block of $G^{22}_{n,p}=V^{\mathsf T}G_{n-1,p}V+\alpha_{n,p}G_{n-1,p-1}$ is $\delta B$. Its first term is $(V^{11})^{\mathsf T}AV^{11}+(V^{11})^{\mathsf T}AV_0V^{21}+(V^{21})^{\mathsf T}V_0^{\mathsf T}AV^{11}+(V^{21})^{\mathsf T}(V_0^{\mathsf T}AV_0+\alpha_{n-1,p}B)V^{21}$. Substituting $V^{11}=-V_0V^{21}$ makes the coefficients of $(V^{21})^{\mathsf T}V_0^{\mathsf T}AV_0V^{21}$ equal $1-1-1+1=0$ and leaves $\alpha_{n-1,p}(V^{21})^{\mathsf T}BV^{21}=\alpha_{n-1,p}^{-1}B$. The first block of $G_{n-1,p-1}$ is $B$, so cancelling invertible $B$ gives $\alpha_{n,p}=\delta-1/\alpha_{n-1,p}$.

The quantum-integer recurrence [F5] solves this scalar recurrence as $\alpha_{n,p}=[n-2p+2]_q/[n-2p+1]_q$: the boundary value at $n=2p$ is $[2]_q/[1]_q=\delta$, and if $\alpha_{n-1,p}=[n-2p+1]_q/[n-2p]_q$, then $\delta-1/\alpha_{n-1,p}=\delta-[n-2p]_q/[n-2p+1]_q=[n-2p+2]_q/[n-2p+1]_q$.

The determinant of the orthogonal block form in step 3.1 and its unit-determinant basis change gives $\det G_{n,p}=([n-2p+2]_q/[n-2p+1]_q)^{d_{n-1,p-1}}\det G_{n-1,p}\det G_{n-1,p-1}$ for $n>2p$, while step 3.2 gives $\det G_{2p,p}=\delta^{d_{2p-1,p-1}}\det G_{2p-1,p-1}$; also $\det G_{n,0}=1$ by step 2.1.

Let $P_{n,p}=\prod_{j=1}^p([n-2p+1+j]_q/[j]_q)^{d_{n,p-j}}$. For $n>2p$, put $h=n-2p+1$. If $p=1$, $P_{n,1}=([h+1]/[h])P_{n-1,1}$. If $p\ge2$, the numerator $[h+j]$ for $2\le j<p$ receives exponents $d_{n-1,p-j-1}$ and $d_{n-1,p-j}$ from the two lower-rank products, summing to $d_{n,p-j}$; at $j=1$ the missing exponent is supplied by $([h+1]/[h])^{d_{n-1,p-1}}$, whose denominator cancels the extra $[h]$, and at $j=p$ the second lower-rank product supplies exponent $d_{n,0}=1$. The denominator exponents add as $d_{n-1,p-j}+d_{n-1,p-j-1}=d_{n,p-j}$ (with the endpoint $j=p$ supplied by the first lower-rank product). Thus $P_{n,p}$ satisfies the recurrence in step 7.1 by Pascal's identity for $d_{n,r}$.

At $n=2p$, $P_{2,1}=[2]=\delta$ for $p=1$. For $p\ge2$, compare net exponents of each quantum integer in $P_{2p,p}$ and $[2]^{d_{2p-1,p-1}}P_{2p-1,p-1}$: for $2\le m\le p$ the exponent is $d_{2p,p-m+1}-d_{2p,p-m}=d_{2p-1,p-m+1}-d_{2p-1,p-m-1}$ by Pascal's identity, exactly the exponent supplied by the latter product; for $m=p+1$ both exponents are $d_{2p,0}=d_{2p-1,0}=1$, and $[1]=1$. Hence $P_{2p,p}=\delta^{d_{2p-1,p-1}}P_{2p-1,p-1}$, the boundary recurrence in step 7.1.

Induction using steps 7.1–8.2 now gives $\det G_{n,p}=P_{n,p}$ for every $q^2$ not a root of unity. Every Gram entry is polynomial in $\delta$, so its determinant is polynomial; the displayed product is rational in $q$ and agrees with that determinant on the infinite set where $q^2$ is not a root of unity. After putting the difference over a common denominator, its polynomial numerator has infinitely many zeros and is identically zero. Thus each displayed zero-over-zero value has the unique removable continuation given by the Gram determinant, proving the formula for every $q\in\mathbb C^\times$.

derivations.claim: Write $d_t=\dim_{\mathbb C}W_{n,t}$. By [F1] and [F3], $\dim\mathrm{TL}_n=\sum_t d_t^2$. By [F2], each simple module is exactly one $D_{n,t}$ with nonzero form quotient, and these modules are pairwise nonisomorphic. If $\phi_{n,t}$ is degenerate then either it is identically zero, so $\dim D_{n,t}=0<d_t$, or its radical is nonzero, so again $\dim D_{n,t}<d_t$.

Suppose $\mathrm{TL}_n$ is semisimple. By [F4] and [F6], every finite-dimensional division algebra factor over $\mathbb C$ is $\mathbb C$: left multiplication by any element has a complex eigenvalue, and a nonzero element of a division algebra is invertible, so the eigenvalue equation forces that element to be scalar. Hence $\dim\mathrm{TL}_n$ is the sum of the squares of the dimensions of its pairwise nonisomorphic simple modules. By [F2], these are the $D_{n,t}$. If any form were degenerate, step 1.1 would make this sum strictly smaller than $\sum_t d_t^2=\dim\mathrm{TL}_n$, a contradiction. Thus all forms are nondegenerate.

Conversely suppose every form is nondegenerate. Then [F2] gives $D_{n,t}=W_{n,t}$ for every $t$, so [F3] says that the squares of the dimensions of the complete simple-module list sum to $\dim\mathrm{TL}_n$. By [F5], the quotient by the Jacobson radical is semisimple and has the same simple modules: the radical annihilates every simple module, so simple modules of the quotient and of the algebra coincide. Applying the division-ring argument in step 2.1 to this semisimple quotient shows that its dimension is the sum of the squares of those simple dimensions. Therefore the quotient has the same dimension as $\mathrm{TL}_n$, the radical has dimension zero, and $\mathrm{TL}_n$ is semisimple.

Case $\ell=1$. Then $q=\pm1$ and $[r]_q=rq^{r-1}\ne0$ for every positive $r$ by [F3]. Every Gram determinant in [F1] is nonzero, so [F2] gives semisimplicity at every rank.

Case $3\le\ell<\infty$ and $n<\ell$. For every allowed $p$, each denominator index $j$ and each numerator index $n-2p+1+j$ in [F1] is positive and less than $\ell$. Neither vanishes by [F3], so all forms are nondegenerate and [F2] gives semisimplicity.

Case $3\le\ell<\infty$ and $n\ge\ell$. Write $n=a\ell+s$ with $a\ge1$ and $0\le s<\ell$. If $s=0$, take $p=j=1$; if $1\le s\le\ell-2$, take $p=j=s+1$; if $s=\ell-1$, take $p=\ell-1,j=\ell-2$. In every case $1\le j\le p<\ell$ and $p\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$: for $s=0$, $p=1$ and $n\ge3$; for $1\le s\le\ell-2$, $2p=2s+2\le\ell+s\le n$; and for $s=\ell-1$, $2p=2\ell-2\le2\ell-1\le n$. Direct substitution gives $n-2p+1+j=a\ell$. The exponent $d_{n,p-j}$ is positive because $p-j$ is $0$ or $1$, and $[j]_q\ne0$ because $j<\ell$. Thus the determinant in [F1] is zero, one form is degenerate, and [F2] gives nonsemisimplicity.

Case $\ell=2$. At $n=0$, $\mathrm{TL}_0=\mathbb C$ is semisimple. For even $n\ge2$, $p=j=1$ gives $\det G_{n,1}=[n]_q/[1]_q=0$, so [F2] gives nonsemisimplicity. If $n$ is odd, then $n-2p+1=2m>0$ for every allowed $p$. For odd $j$, both quantum integers in each factor of [F1] are nonzero; for $j=2k$, numerator and denominator have simple zeros at $q^2=-1$, and their ratio tends to $(-1)^m(m+k)/k\ne0$. Hence all continued determinants are nonzero and [F2] gives semisimplicity for odd $n$.

The cases $\ell=\infty$, $\ell=1$, $3\le\ell<\infty$ with $n<\ell$ or $n\ge\ell$, and $\ell=2$ exhaust all possibilities. Steps 1.1–1.5 prove exactly the branches in the Statement, including the rank-zero order-two endpoint.

Fix $r\ge2$ and assume inductively that through rank $r$ the recursively defined elements are nonzero idempotents, are annihilated on both sides by every generator, have corner $\mathbb C p_s$, and satisfy $\tau_s(p_s)=[s+1]/\delta^s$.

Put $P=p_r\otimes1$, $Q=p_{r-1}\otimes1\otimes1$, $a=d_{r-1}$, $b=d_r$, and $\mu=[r-1]/[r]$. The recursion at rank $r$ gives $P=Q-\mu QaQ$; $Q$ is idempotent, commutes with $b$, and $bab=b$ by [F1]. Therefore $bPb=\delta Qb-\mu QbabQ=(\delta-\mu)Qb=([r+1]/[r])Qb$ by [F3].

Set $X=PbP$ and $c=[r]/[r+1]$. Since $PQ=QP=P$, step 3.1 gives $X^2=P(bPb)P=([r+1]/[r])X$, so $(P-cX)^2=P-cX=p_{r+1}$. Also $bp_{r+1}=bP-cbPbP=0$ by step 3.1 and $QbP=bP$; and $p_{r+1}b=Pb-cPbPb=0$ because $PbPb=P(bPb)=([r+1]/[r])PQb=([r+1]/[r])Pb$. For $i<r$, both annihilation identities follow from the induction hypothesis. The correction term has fewer than $r+1$ through strands by [F6], so the coefficient of the identity diagram in $p_{r+1}$ is $1$ and $p_{r+1}\ne0$.
Every nonempty generator word has a rightmost letter which kills $p_{r+1}$ by step 4.1. Since generator words span $\mathrm{TL}_{r+1}$ by [F5], $p_{r+1}\mathrm{TL}_{r+1}p_{r+1}=\mathbb C p_{r+1}$.

By [F4], $\tau_{r+1}(P)=\tau_r(p_r)$ and, using cyclicity, $\tau_{r+1}(X)=\tau_{r+1}(PbP)=\tau_{r+1}(bP^2)=\tau_{r+1}(Pb)=\delta^{-1}\tau_r(p_r)$. Hence $\tau_{r+1}(p_{r+1})=\tau_r(p_r)(1-[r]/(\delta[r+1]))=[r+2]/\delta^{r+1}$ by [F3] and the induction hypothesis. This proves the trace recurrence and closes the induction.

The product can be chosen so that no intermediate stack creates a closed cycle. Therefore the set of diagrams lies in the unital subalgebra of $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ generated by these diagrams.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and let $\delta\in R$. The object labels are the nonnegative integers $n=0,1,2,\ldots$. For labels $m,n$, place bottom points $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ and top points $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ along the rectangle from left to right on their respective edges. Their cyclic order is $t_1,\ldots,t_n,b_m,\ldots,b_1$. When $m=n=0$, the empty matching is included.

For every commutative ring $R$, loop value $\delta\in R$, and objects $m,n,p,q\ge0$, the raw diagram data of [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]] form a strict monoidal category $\mathcal{TL}_R(\delta)$ with hom-modules $M_R(m,n)$ and the stated $R$-bilinear stacking composition. Composition is associative, the identity diagrams are two-sided identities, and horizontal juxtaposition is a strict monoidal bifunctor with unit object $0$. Consequently $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{TL}_R(\delta)}(n)=\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ is a unital associative $R$-algebra whose underlying $R$-module is free on its noncrossing pairing diagrams.

derivations.claim: A basis diagram has $n$ propagating strands exactly when it is the identity. If either factor in a product has fewer than $n$ propagating strands, every exterior through path in the product must pass through a distinct propagating path in that factor; hence the product also has fewer than $n$. Thus the span of nonidentity diagrams is a two-sided ideal and $\varepsilon$ is an algebra homomorphism. Its kernel is spanned by nonempty generator words by [F1].

If $K_\varepsilon$ is projective, the surjection $\varepsilon:A\to K_\varepsilon$ splits as a left $A$-module map $s$. Put $e=s(1)$. Then $\varepsilon(e)=1$ and, for every $a\in A$, $ae=s(\varepsilon(a))=\varepsilon(a)e$. Taking $a=e$ gives $e^2=e$, and taking $a=d_i$ gives $d_i e=0$.

Conversely suppose $e\ne0$, $e^2=e$, and $d_i e=0$ for every generator. Every nonempty generator word kills $e$ by its rightmost letter, so [F1] gives $ae=\varepsilon(a)e$ for all $a\in A$. If $\varepsilon(e)=0$, then $e\in\ker\varepsilon$ is a linear combination of nonempty generator words, whence $e^2=0$, contradicting $e^2=e\ne0$. Thus $\varepsilon(e)=1$, and $s:K_\varepsilon\to A$, $s(\lambda)=\lambda e$, is an $A$-linear section of $\varepsilon$. Hence $K_\varepsilon$ is a direct summand of the free left regular module and is projective.
Steps 2.1 and 2.2 prove both implications and the normalization $\varepsilon(e)=1$. No uniqueness assertion is needed for this projectivity equivalence.

By [F2], $\tau_2(u)=1$, while $\tau_2(1)=1$. The trace-pairing matrix in the basis $\{1,u\}$ is therefore $$\begin{pmatrix}\tau_2(1)&\tau_2(u)\\ \tau_2(u)&\tau_2(u^2)\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},$$ whose nonzero vector $1-u$ pairs to zero with both basis vectors.
